result.summary: Two short fragments credit the Idaean Dactyls with early metalworking. One says they taught iron smelting and tempering in Crete; the other names Celmis and Damnameneus as discoverers of iron in Cyprus and Delas, or Scythes, as discoverer of bronze smelting.

scenes.title: Dactyls teach ironworking in Crete
scenes.summary: Pliny reports that Hesiod says the Idaean Dactyls taught the smelting and tempering of iron in Crete.

scenes.title: Discovery of iron and bronze
scenes.summary: Clement says Celmis and Damnameneus discovered iron in Cyprus, and Delas, called Scythes by Hesiod, discovered bronze smelting.

alias_notes.explanation: Hesiod, according to Clement, calls the Idaean Delas by the name Scythes.

analysis.text: The fragments show Greek myth attributing the origins of technology, here metalworking, to semi-divine beings rather than to human invention.

The fragments are quoted by later writers, Pliny and Clement, who cite Hesiod on the origins of crafts. The competing claims for Crete and Cyprus reflect the importance of both islands in ancient metal trade and lore.

fun_facts.text: The name Dactyls means fingers in Greek, and they were linked with Mount Ida in Crete.

language_notes.text: "Dactyls" comes from the Greek for "fingers"; the Idaean Dactyls were mythical beings linked with Mount Ida and metalworking.
"Tempering" means hardening metal by heating and then cooling it in a controlled way.
"Scythes[1501]" – the bracketed number is an editorial footnote marker, not part of the ancient text.

context_notes.text: Pliny the Elder, a Roman author, wrote the encyclopedic Natural History in the first century AD, quoting Hesiod secondhand.
Clement of Alexandria was a Christian writer around AD 200; his Stromateis lists inventors, drawing on earlier Greek sources.
